title: Reasoning by analogy
hook: extending a ruling to a new case by a shared reason

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was ijma', the agreement of the scholars, and your line was agreement. Did you learn one ruling the scholars agree on? Day one thousand one hundred seventy-two.

A woman from the tribe of Juhayna comes to the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, with a question about her mother, who had vowed to make the pilgrimage, and died before she could go. May the daughter go for her? The answer, in Sahih al-Bukhari, is yes. But the way he answers is what matters today. He asks her a question back: if your mother had owed a debt, would you have paid it? Yes, she says. Then pay what is owed to Allah, he says, for Allah has more right to be paid. One case she understood, a debt, carried over to a case she didn't, by what the two shared. Today's word is that move.
screen: `A MOTHER'S VOW, UNFULFILLED.` → `WOULD YOU PAY HER DEBT?` → `THEN PAY THIS ONE.`

segments.voice: The word is qiyas, measuring one thing against another. In Sunni legal theory it names a way of reaching a ruling for a new case that no text addresses directly, by finding an old case that a text does address and a reason the two share. The books of legal theory name its parts. The original case, the asl, the root. The new case, the far', the branch. The shared reason, the 'illa, the cause behind the ruling. And the ruling itself, the hukm, which travels from root to branch along that reason. An example the books of legal theory reach for is wine. The Qur'an names strong drink among the things believers are told to leave aside, in Surah al-Ma'idah, verse ninety. Jurists asked what it is about wine that carries the ruling. Not the grape. Not the color. The intoxication. So when a drink made from something else intoxicates in the same way, the ruling reaches it too, by likeness. A hadith in Sahih Muslim says the same thing directly, that every intoxicant is forbidden, and jurists treat that report as its own text; the wine case is still a way the books teach the method. Notice what qiyas is not. It isn't a hunch, and it isn't a new law out of nowhere. It has to start from a text and travel only as far as the reason travels. If the shared reason is wrong, the analogy fails, and much of the scholars' arguing is over exactly that. And not every school uses it the same way. The Hanafi, Maliki, Shafi'i and Hanbali schools count it as a source. Ja'fari jurists, of the Shia, do not reason by analogy in this way; they give reason its own place, and that is tomorrow.
screen: `QIYAS: MEASURING ONE BY ANOTHER.` · `ROOT, BRANCH, REASON, RULING.` · `WINE, AND THE REASON BEHIND IT.` · `THE SCHOOLS DON'T ALL USE IT.`

segments.voice: The practice: one analogy, done slowly. Take a rule you already keep. Say, you don't read someone's private messages. Ask what the reason is. Maybe that they're theirs, and they didn't open them to you. Now find a new case that shares the reason. A diary left on a table. A notebook in a borrowed bag. Does the reason travel? Then the rule travels with it. If it doesn't, notice what stopped it. If you pray, you can ask for clear sight. If not, just sit with your one root and its branch. The bell holds the time.
Qiyas. Reasoning by analogy: a ruling carried from an old case to a new one, along the reason they share. Today's word.
Your line: by likeness. Today, when you meet something new, ask what it is like, and why. Name the shared reason before you carry anything over. Day one thousand one hundred seventy-two.

howItsDone: In the Hanafi, Maliki, Shafi'i and Hanbali schools, jurists use analogy to rule on cases no text names, by finding a shared reason with a case a text does name; Ja'fari jurists do not reason by analogy in this way.

fork.setup: a daughter asks the Prophet whether she may make the pilgrimage her late mother vowed. how does he answer?
options: he tells her a vow ends with the one who made it.
he asks whether she would pay her mother's debt.
he tells her to ask the scholars of her tribe.
fork.reveal: he asks about a debt. she would pay it, so, he says, pay what is owed to Allah. the answer is yes, reached by likeness.

original.note: Arabic: measuring one thing against another; in law, reasoning by analogy.

trapdoor: what you thought: qiyas is guessing what the rule probably is.
what it means: carrying a ruling from a case a text names to a new case, along a reason the two share.
what a scholar hears: asl, far', 'illa, hukm. the arguments live in the 'illa: get the reason wrong and the whole analogy fails.

sources.ref: Sahih al-Bukhari 1852 (the woman of Juhayna and her mother's vow of pilgrimage)

notes: Bukhari 1852: confirm number and paraphrase (debt analogy; 'Allah has more right to be paid').
Four parts of qiyas (asl, far', 'illa, hukm) and the wine/intoxication example as the standard teaching example: confirm wording; 'the example the books of legal theory reach for' is a general claim.
Muslim 2003 (kullu muskirin haram): confirm number; the script notes jurists treat it as its own text so the wine analogy is presented as a teaching illustration.
Gloss of qiyas as 'measuring one thing against another': confirm against a standard lexicon.
Ja'fari jurists rejecting qiyas (in the Sunni sense): confirm framing is fair; some Ja'fari jurists accept analogy where the cause is stated in the text (mansus al-'illa). Consider adding nuance.
